title: Today in one sentence
text: Markets open Monday after a rough Friday, when the Nasdaq 100 fund QQQ fell 2.5% and chip maker AMD fell 6.0%; at the open, watch whether tech stocks keep sliding or settle down, and keep an eye on interest rates, because the Fed meets October 27 and 28.

title: Tech and chips start the week down
text: On Friday, Meta fell 3.7%, Broadcom 4.5%, Vertiv 3.9% and Rocket Lab 8.0%. These companies are tied to the AI boom, so they often rise and fall together. Mondays can bring a bounce or more selling, and nobody can know which one in advance.

title: Steadier areas held up
text: Lockheed Martin rose 3.7% and the dividend fund SCHD rose 0.7% on Friday, while energy was the best sector on the Nasdaq (up 1.6%). When one corner of the market gets nervous, other corners often act differently, which is the idea behind mixing industries.

title: Lockheed reports on October 22
text: Lockheed Martin has said it will publish quarterly results before the market opens on Thursday, October 22. Report days can bring big moves, up or down, because real numbers replace guesses.

title: The Fed meets October 27 and 28
text: The 10 year Treasury yield is near 5.1%, and a hotter than expected inflation report last week made another rate hike a real possibility. Reports differ on how likely it is. Higher rates make borrowing costlier and make safe bonds more attractive, which can weigh on stocks.

title: Lesson 12: What is market capitalization?
text: Market capitalization, or market cap, is the total price tag the stock market puts on a whole company. You get it by multiplying the share price by the number of shares. For example, Nvidia is worth about $5.2 trillion, while Rocket Lab is worth about $30 billion. A share price alone does not tell you which company is bigger: a $1,257 share of Eli Lilly and a $50 share of Rocket Lab come from companies of very different sizes. Bigger companies often swing less than small ones, but not always. This is for learning, not advice to buy or sell anything.
